newsitem.title: USA: UPS, Teamsters reach deal to end strike.
newsitem.headline: UPS, Teamsters reach deal to end strike.

text.p: United Parcel Service, the world's largest parcel delivery company, has reached a tentative agreement to end a 15-day Teamsters strike that crippled the delivery of packages nationwide, Labor Secretary Alexis Herman said early on Tuesday.
"I am pleased to announce that the United Parcel Service and the Teamsters union have reached a tentative settlement," she told a news conference shortly after midnight.
The strike by 185,000 Teamsters had crippled the world's largest carrier of small packages, costing UPS $650 million in lost business.

Ron Carey, president of the International Brotherhood of Teamsters, said the union had turned back the company's initial demand to pull out of the Teamsters multi-employer pension plans and start a new pension plan.
"This is not just a Teamster victory, this is a victory for all working people," he told a follow-up news conference at Teamsters headquarters.
Carey said workers might start returning to work as early as Wednesday night, even though a formal ratification vote would take longer.
President Bill Clinton patted both sides on the back in an early-morning statement read to reporters in Edgartown, Mass., where he was on vacation.

"Today's agreement represents their hard work and determination to reconcile their differences for the good of the company, its employees and the customers they serve," Clinton said. "The issues that were at the heart of their negotiations are important to our nation's economic strength, and to all Americans."

Carey said he expected the company to carry out at least some temporary layoffs while its business begins to return to normal. Before the strike began Aug. 4, UPS handled 12 million items on a normal weekday.
The chief UPS negotiator, Dave Murray, joined Carey in paying tribute to Herman, the labor secretary, for having nursed the contract talks to a successful conclusion.
Herman said the company and the union had created together "a model workplace" for the 21st century.
The two sides had begun their latest round of talks Thursday at the request of Herman. The talks continued for more than 80 hours, except for brief sleep breaks.
The strike involved more workers than any other walkout in over a decade.
